posts.caption: The farrier's truck pulled in at 6:40 and the whole barn went quiet. He had a full schedule, a thermos, and a patient face. My big mare had her own plan, which involved leaning every one of her 1,400 pounds into his shoulder. We tried carrots, then a firm voice, then the carrots again. Forty minutes later he had two shoes on and a new respect for the word negotiation. He wrote the visit down as a team effort, which was kind. She stood at the end looking like she'd won a small war, and I suppose she had.
posts.first: I keep a jar of peppermints on the shelf by the farrier's spot, and I've never told him it's a bribe. He's never asked. Last month he left a wrapper in the aisle and I kept it. It's in the drawer with the hoof pick and the receipts.

posts.caption: I put the blanket on him at six in the morning because the forecast said freezing rain. It was a good blanket, navy with a reflective strip, and it fit him nearly perfectly. He stood still for the buckles and even lowered his head to help. I walked back up to the house for coffee. By the time I came out again, the paddock had turned to soup and he was standing in the middle of it like a small brown monument. The blanket survived. Mostly. We keep a washing machine at the barn for this reason.
posts.first: My husband built me a blanket rack last spring so I could keep them dry between wears. It holds four blankets. We own eleven. The other seven live on the trunk, the fence, and a chair in the tack room that nobody is allowed to sit in.

posts.quote: Every barn has one bucket nobody owns, nobody fills, and nobody has ever once been able to throw away.
posts.first: There's a green bucket in our aisle that's been there since the barn was built. It's cracked, it's missing a handle, and it has held water, grain, soaking hay, and one very confused kitten. I've threatened to replace it three times. Nobody has let me finish the sentence.

posts.caption: First cold night of the year, I walked down to the barn with a pot of mash and a headlamp that was dying. Every stall was quiet, and the string lights over the aisle were doing their usual little glow. I stood there longer than I needed to, listening to hay being chewed in the dark. The barn cat appeared out of nowhere and climbed onto the nearest warm back. She has opinions about which horse, and I stopped arguing years ago. The mash was gone in four minutes, and so was my plan to get anything else done.
posts.first: My mother had a rule that you feed the animals before you feed yourself. I used to think it was about being tough. Now I think it was about the best part of the evening being down at the barn, quiet, before anyone needed anything from you.

posts.caption: Her birthday is in April, and every year I forget to count. The vet's office keeps a file with the real number, and I keep a smaller, kinder number in my head. She has never once objected. She walks the fence line every morning with her chin up, checks the gate, checks me, and heads for the hay like a woman with a train to catch. Last week I found a white hair in her mane and moved it out of sight. We've both agreed the file is private. The hay remains the main topic.
posts.first: I used to dye my own hair on the back porch every six weeks. These days I tell people the barn dust does it for me. The mare and I have an arrangement. Neither of us announces anything, and both of us go to bed early.

posts.caption: The mailbox at the end of our lane is dented from the day the school bus clipped it in 2016. It's also the most feared object on the farm. Every new horse gets the same tour and the same reaction: ears locked, nostrils wide, a polite shuffle sideways. The old gelding stands at the fence and watches them go through it. He doesn't comment. He leans on the post a little harder, like a man at a bus stop who has seen this show before. The mailman waves at him every day, and he waves back with one ear.
posts.first: Our mail comes around noon, and the old boy is at the fence by 11:50 every day. I don't think he cares about the mail. I think he likes being there when something shows up. He did it again today. I brought him a peppermint. The mail was a catalog.
